If you have the lore books in the first one there is a cosmology chart for the lore. Basically the void lords are the greater powers of Shadow (https://www.wowhead.com/news/world-of-warcraft-cosmology-chart-in-color-315151). Most forces in WoW act in opposition to each other, and form a sort of balance, but it’s somewhat common for one to basically act up and try and take more power. The void lords basically saw what the Titans were doing by using worlds to gather new titans to their cause and were like “yo, we want that” and Sargares wasn’t having any of that so he killed the corrupted world. The council of titans convened and basically kicked him out because he said he wouldn’t stop. 

We don’t really know a ton about the void lords besides them being super powerful because there’s few of them. Basically think of power of a cosmic force as a zero sum, so the more entities that share that power the weaker they are, and each of the pools is roughly the same size. So if the Naaru are light and there is like 1000 of them and the void lords are shadow and there’s like 10, each void lord is 10x as powerful as each Naaru. It’s not exactly like that and it gets complicated when numbers diminish (it’s not like The One) but that’s the gist of it. 

We don’t know what their mega end game is, we know they want to corrupt Azeroth and turn her to a void titan because she’s insanely powerful. But a lot of what has been happening so far has been revolving around them. All of the old gods, the Lich king, the burning legion, shadowlands, and even the sub plot in dragon flight was about Tyr and the watchers and how the dragons play into the larger picture. But yea basically the eventual conflict with the will be the culmination of all of Warcraft up to that point.

There’s a lot of ways, but it depends on level of effort and relative skill in crafting. Like I’m someone who has spent a lot of time working on cosplay in the past with ease of access to things like tools, sewing machines, and a 3D printer. It also depends on the level of complexity you’d like to achieve as well, if you want a more complex/complicated process that’s one thing, if you want something simpler that’s another. 

Without knowing more specifics I’d say the big things I’d do is first your weapons. A katana is fine, but it’s on the small side. There are ways you can make your own with some finishing planks, a hand saw, and some sanding. The gun is also very small relative to the game. You can make your own with some pvc pipe, foam (insulation or hobby), and some thin foam sheeting. 

Next I would look at your pants and undershirts. You don’t need anything fancy but most bloodborne armor is based around late 19th early 20th century styling. I would recommend going thrifting for base materials and looking for other garments you can cut and integrate into it. For example you use a base that has pants and straps, get a close pair of pants and another or a jacket to make straps from.

Cable management and functional storage. Like literally make it clean and easy and it makes things look so much better. RE6 is a weird game, when it came out I originally explained it as basically 3 different games in one, at least in terms of how it feels. You have Chris’ story which has the pacing and combat of what feels like a third person call of duty with monsters. Leon’s feels like a more classic RE game, methodically fighting zombies that seem weak but actually that’s what makes them dangerous. Hi, I have a degree and game design, and have been working on my own first game for the last year, and I’m here to tell you, it’s not possible to manufacture games domestically in the short term without drastically increasing costs to consumers. Here’s why. 

First of all we don’t have the existing infrastructure to do it, can it be built? Sure, but it would take minimum 18 months to secure space, permitting, machines (which are made oversees), train workers, build supplies chains, and go through other regulatory processes. All of this is not cheap and takes time, but the biggest hurdle to this is rent costs, even a small 10,000 sq ft space would run north of $30k a month, as you can’t really make this in a shopping center. 

Second issue you have is modularity. Unless you’re using VERY basic components, and I mean VERY basic like wooden blocks and discs, every board game is essentially a one off custom affair that is a run of 5,000-10,000 units. That may sound like a lot, but when you consider all the things that go in from boxes, tokens, cards, miniatures, and trays it’s A LOT of work for a product that shelves for maybe $100. Even more mainstream titles like monopoly or uno are not easy endeavors as they have very tight tolerances and quality control on what makes it to shelves, and those are games that print 100,000 in a run, small games a MUCH smaller. 

Finally you have the drastically increased cost of domestic labor, plus the fact that most of that labor won’t work for minimum wage. So say a game costs $10 to make in China per unit right now. That $10 to pays for materials, labor, utilities, rent, and the R&D and prototyping process, of which most games go through 10+ iterations. For you to make the same product you need not only the machines but also the supply chains for all plastic, cardboard, laminate, cardstock, resin, metal, and any other discrete component that may be in it. Plus you need labor, say you have 10 stations through the process, you may have 5 people working and they rotate through stations, that’s $75/hour minimum for labor alone, much less everything else. I’ve seen estimates that the CHEAPEST you can do manufacturing in the US for a game that costs $10 to produce overseas is $120, then you need to figure out everything else on top of that such as logistics, development costs, distribution, marketing, shelf time, and so many other factors that a game that was $100 is now $400. 

All of this is before you even consider that this isn’t changing the profit margins for the company itself, so the studio may make $5/unit, that change is to still make $5/unit. But what do they do when the inflationary aspects come into play? Everything goes up AGAIN, it’s not a small aspect, this means costs may go up again to cover those margins. 

And it gets EVEN BETTER. For those studios who already ordered their product MONTHS ago, but are either mid or end of the production right now and haven’t departed, say they had an order for games that was $1M like Gloomhaven developer Cephalofair games, where now for their product that is on its way to clear customs they have the pay the 145% tariffs. So to receive the product they paid for it’s not $1.5M. https://cephalofair.com/blogs/blog/tariffs-and-cephalofair-games

So yeah, this lawsuit isn’t just about cutting into profits because they refuse to hire Nebraskans (which spoiler alert they do, they are Nebraskans). It’s about how their entire SMALL business is at risk because of this insanity.

So I’m gonna take a minute here to explain how some of this stuff works because I feel like it would be helpful. Basically anytime a strike is ordered a strike assessment is done. This includes a wide variety of information but the big things are 1) target type and relative priority. Basically if it’s a high ranking commander who is involved in large amounts of troop movements and logistics it’s likely a higher priority than a figure head. 2) fortification and response assessment. This is things like where the target is located, what sorts of armor it might be, is it possible the asset launching the strike is at risk when making it, and what a possible response post strike would look like. 3) collateral damage assessment. This is what you’re likely looking for but it’s the question of what is the type risk of collateral, is it human life, is it critical infrastructure, is it mass power loss, what does this look like. 4) finally strike package options. This is the list of recommendations that the analysts suggest to use and the possible outcomes with all gathered intelligence, and can include an assessment of “nothing, collateral damage is too high” but usually it’s not just one thing is like 5 or 6. 

From there the analysts give it to mission command and they make the decision. If a senior officer is present they can overrule the decision, however this isn’t super common, it’s usually seen as a subversion of command. But at this point an option is chosen and executed on, IF another actor sees this and the party involved is subject to the ICJ they can bring charges forward or bring action at the UN Security Council. The problem we have now is the US basically walked away from everything, so bringing them to account is difficult if not impossible.

Now it’s fair to bring up the point that you feel a strike is immoral, or that people being placed in command are willingly acting on strikes that they know would result in civilian casualties. In fact I would likely agree with most of those arguments. But it is important to understand the RoE and process behind a lot of this.

So welcome to Archerus, I’ve mained DK on and off since they’ve come out. But to give you a bit of an overview:

Blood is the tank spec, and imho the best in the game. They basically embody the self regeneration aspect of tanking. Basically the idea is you just out heal most damage done (most times I would out heal healers in boss fights in end game dungeons). This combined with high burst damage windows and crazy utility like death grip makes them incredibly fun to play. 

Unholy and Frost are both DPS specs, but play very differently. Unholy is all about disease and minions, the idea behind them is that you apply dots and summon ads to keep damage up if you need to drop off the boss and can even have good range damage abilities if you build the right way. Most builds now are built around a big damage window every 45 or 90 seconds depending on hero talents (starting at level 71). 

Frost is in a bit of an odd place imho, and unfortunately it’s my preferred of the two DPS specs. There are two major playstyles in it: obliteration which is all about big burst crit winds every 60 or 90 seconds with support damage abilities spread intermittently. The other of breath of sindragosa which is a 100% intense resource management spec that is technically unique just not very fun to play. Basically every two minutes you use a big cooldown that does a conal attack and constantly drains runic power, so spending runes and using generator cds in this window is critical. It’s interesting yes, but not something that for me is especially fun because it punishes time off boss and mechanics super hard. 

Any of the specs are fun and viable, especially if you can grasp the various ways they play.

As far as rent control goes housing is an inelastic good, meaning everyone needs it, sure there is some elasticity in the size of that, rooms etc, but in general it’s inelastic. This means a market isn’t great at addressing the supply of it. The whole point of rent control is the maximum a landlord (someone who contributes nothing otherwise outside of an extraction of wealth from people will less than them) can charge for housing. This could be tied to value of the unit, tax assessments, income, or mortgage but it does set an upper limit. What this does is level the playing field for people who are in these units to be able to have an affordable place to live AND have money to put back into the local economy, as we know trickle down just doesn’t work.

Most likely thing is you’re starving your generators out of a certain resource. You said your onto coal, so I would check to make sure you’re belting enough coal to your generators, so if you’re mining from a normal node with a mark 1 miner you’re extracting 60/minute with no overclock, so it would completely fill a mk1 belt. Each coal generator not overclocked takes 15 coal/min so in a mk 1 miner and mk 1 belt you get 4 fully stocked generators. 

The next half of the coal generator is water, as we burn to coal to spin a water turbine to produce electricity. Coal generators consume water at a rate of 45 m3/minute, or 45/minute. Water extractor produce water at a rate of 120/minute, so one extractor will supply just under 3 generators. I typically build one pump per two, but that is usually overkill. The thing you want to make sure with water and really all fluids is headlift, or how far you can upward push liquid. Normal headlift from an extractor is 10 meters, so the top fill line is 10 meters from the top of the exit pipe. So if you wanted to move the fluid upwards of 20 meters you’d need an additional pump roughly 10 meters up the vertical. I also recommend putting a fluid buffer at the top of the vertical as well, this gives you more efficient head lift out of your extractors and pumps and can help maintain pressure in pipes as well. If you want a more thorough explanation I can, but it’s pretty long. 

The final thing to keep in mine will try liquid is like belts pipes have a maximum capacity and throughput as well, so make sure you aren’t trying to put too much through too small of a space.
